title: North Sikkim History: Lepcha Dzongu, Dzumsa and the Lake
meta_description: The story of North Sikkim: Kabi Lungchok's oath, the Lepcha reserve of Dzongu, the Dzumsa councils of Lachung and Lachen, Gurudongmar lore and the 2023 flood.
summary: North Sikkim holds Sikkim's founding oath at Kabi Lungchok, the Lepcha reserve of Dzongu, and two Bhutia villages, Lachung and Lachen, that still govern themselves through the Dzumsa. Gurudongmar Lake carries the lore of Guru Padmasambhava. The October 2023 Teesta flood is the newest chapter, and it still shapes travel here.

sections.heading: An oath at Kabi Lungchok
paras: Drive 17 km north of Gangtok and you reach a grove of cypress with standing stones beside the road. This is Kabi Lungchok, and the story told here is the one Sikkim tells about its own beginning. In the 13th century, the account goes, Khye Bumsa, a prince from Kham in eastern Tibet, came south and met the Lepcha chief and seer Thekong Tek. The two swore blood brotherhood, binding Lepcha and Bhutia as one people, and the stones mark the place.

The descendants of Khye Bumsa became the Namgyal dynasty, and in 1642 Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated the first Chogyal of Sikkim at Yuksom. For our purposes the important point is that the north of Sikkim was never an empty frontier. It was Lepcha country first, then a Lepcha and Bhutia country under the Chogyals, whose capital stood at Tumlong, near Phodong, from 1793 until 1894. When you pass through Phodong on the way north, the ruins of that capital are a short climb above the road.

sections.heading: Dzongu, the Lepcha reserve
paras: Lepchas call themselves Mutanchi Rongkup, and their name for this land is Mayel Lyang. Lepcha elders tell that the creator mother Itbu-moo shaped the first man and woman, Fudongthing and Nazaong Nyu, from the snows of Kongchen Konglo, the mountain the rest of the world calls Kanchenjunga. That is why the mountain is their guardian, and why its peaks, lakes and rivers are part of Lepcha prayer. We tell this as Lepcha lore, as it is told in Dzongu homes.

Dzongu, the wedge of valleys across the Teesta from Mangan, was set aside for the Lepchas in the time of the Chogyals, and the protection continued after Sikkim joined India in 1975. Outsiders still need a permit to enter, and land is held by Dzongu Lepchas. That is the reason villages such as Lingthem, Passingdang and Hee Gyathang still speak Lepcha at home and keep their shamans, the bongthing and the mun, alongside Buddhist lamas.

Upper Dzongu holds Tholung Monastery, revealed as a sacred site in 1760 and built in 1789. During the Gorkha invasions, relics from other monasteries were hidden there, and every third year in April they are brought out for the Kamsel display. In 2007 and 2008 Dzongu came to national attention when Lepcha activists of the Affected Citizens of Teesta held a long hunger strike in Gangtok against hydropower projects planned in the reserve; several projects were later dropped.

sections.heading: The Dzumsa of Lachung and Lachen
paras: Above Chungthang the valley forks. The Lachen Chu comes down from the north-west, the Lachung Chu from the north-east, and they meet to form the Teesta. Up each river lies a Bhutia village: Lachen, the big pass, and Lachung, the small pass. Their families traded wool, salt and grain over the high passes into Tibet until 1950, moving with their yaks between summer and winter settlements.

Each village runs itself through the Dzumsa, a council in which every household has a voice. It is led by an elected headman, the Pipon, and it settles disputes, decides grazing rules and the yearly movement of herds, and today sets rules for tourism, waste and land. The system took shape in the first half of the 19th century, and Sikkim's law still lets the Dzumsa stand in place of an elected panchayat in these two villages. As a visitor you feel it in small ways: rules on plastic, on where vehicles park, and on who may buy land, which is no one from outside.

sections.heading: Hooker in the high valleys
paras: In 1849 the botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker walked up both valleys on his Sikkim expedition, collecting rhododendron seed and crossing toward the Donkia pass and the Tibetan plateau. He described Lachung and Lachen in his Himalayan Journals, published in 1854, and many rhododendrons in Victorian gardens grew from seed he sent home. Late in that same year, Hooker and Archibald Campbell, the Superintendent of Darjeeling, were detained by officials of the Sikkim court. Their release was followed by a British annexation of Sikkimese land in the Darjeeling hills. The rhododendrons Hooker admired are the same ones that still flower in the Shingba sanctuary at Yumthang in late April and May.

sections.heading: Gurudongmar, told as lore
paras: Gurudongmar Lake lies at about 5,180 m, a few kilometres south of the Tibetan border. The story most often told in Lachen is Buddhist: Guru Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, who brought Buddhism to the Himalaya in the 8th century, passed this way, and when the herders who came here asked for water in winter, he blessed part of the lake so that it would not freeze. People still point to a patch near the shore that stays open when the rest is ice. This is lore, told with devotion, and we pass it on as that.

Some Sikh traditions tell a different story, linking the lake to Guru Nanak. The competing claims have at times been the subject of local dispute. On the shore today you see prayer flags and a small shrine, and visitors of every faith carry home bottles of the water. Whatever story you hold, the rule is the same: walk quietly, do not throw coins or litter, and remember you are a guest in a place that is sacred to the people who live below it.

sections.heading: The flood of October 2023
paras: On the night of 3–4 October 2023, South Lhonak lake, a glacial lake in the far north-west of the district, burst through its moraine wall after heavy rain. The flood reached Chungthang around midnight, destroyed the Teesta III dam within minutes, and then tore out bridges, houses and long stretches of road down the Teesta valley, including parts of NH10 between Sikkim and Bengal. Many lives were lost, among them soldiers at a camp near Singtam.

Since then, North Sikkim has opened and closed in stages. The Chungthang crossing and the Lachen road have been the slowest to recover, and monsoon landslides have closed them again more than once. Lachung, Lachen and the Dzongu villages have rebuilt with the help of the people who visit. If you go, go knowing this history, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Dzumsa in Lachung and Lachen?
faqs.a: The Dzumsa is the traditional self-government of Lachung and Lachen, a council in which every household has a voice, led by an elected headman called the Pipon. It settles disputes, grazing rules and, today, tourism and waste rules. It took shape in the early 19th century, and Sikkim's law still recognises it in place of a panchayat in these two villages.

faqs.q: Why do you need a permit to enter Dzongu?
faqs.a: Because Dzongu is a protected reserve for the Lepcha people, set aside in the time of the Chogyals and kept after 1975. The permit limits outside settlement and protects Lepcha land, which is held by Dzongu Lepchas. Visitors are welcome in homestays but need the Dzongu permit, usually issued at Mangan. Check current status before you travel.

Kabi Lungchok, 17 km north of Gangtok, is where Sikkim's founding story places the 13th-century blood-brotherhood oath between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa, a prince from eastern Tibet. Stone pillars mark the site. The Namgyal kings of Sikkim traced their line from Khye Bumsa. Indians need no permit to visit.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: The story most told in Lachen is that Guru Padmasambhava blessed part of the lake so it would not freeze in winter, giving herders water. A patch near the shore is said to stay open when the rest is ice. Some Sikh traditions link the lake to Guru Nanak instead. Both are lore, told with devotion.

faqs.q: Who are the Lepchas of Dzongu?
faqs.a: The Lepchas, who call themselves Mutanchi Rongkup, are regarded as the first people of Sikkim. Dzongu is their reserved homeland, where Lepcha is still the home language and shamans called bongthing and mun keep older rites beside Buddhist practice. Their lore holds that the first humans were made from the snows of Kanchenjunga.

On the night of 3–4 October 2023, South Lhonak glacial lake burst after heavy rain. The flood destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang and swept away bridges, homes and road sections down the valley, including parts of NH10. North Sikkim has reopened in stages since, with repeated closures. Check current status before you travel.

Lachung Monastery, a Nyingma gompa on the slope above the village, was founded in 1880, and Lachen Monastery dates from 1858. Both hold yearly masked dances on dates set by the Tibetan calendar, and both are open to respectful visitors. Ask your lodge for the current dance dates, which shift each year.

Yes. The botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker travelled up both the Lachen and Lachung valleys in 1849, collecting rhododendron seed and describing the villages in his Himalayan Journals of 1854. Later that year he and Archibald Campbell were detained by Sikkim court officials, an episode that led to a British annexation of Sikkimese land.

faqs.q: Where was the old capital of Sikkim near North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Tumlong, just above Phodong on the North Sikkim road, about 38 km from Gangtok, was the Chogyals' capital from 1793 until 1894, when the court moved to Gangtok. Little of the palace survives, but the site, Phodong Monastery and Labrang Monastery make a good half-day stop with no permit needed for Indians.
